Fig. 2, represents one of the eight Swedes his subjects […] Fig. 3, is one of sixteen Muscovites, their adversaries […] LAWS. 1. Any piece may move from one square to another in a right line, as from a to c; but not corner-wise […] 3. If the king should stand in b, and no other piece in c, e, or m, he may escape by that road, unless one of the Muscovites immediately gets possession of one of the squares in question […] 9. If any one man gets between two squares occupied by his enemies, he is killed and taken off, except the king, who is not liable to this misfortune. […] 12. Whenever the king is thus taken or imprisoned, the war is over.

records.supportingPassage: The fanorona board is a rectangular parallelogram […] Forty-four movable pieces are required for the game — twenty-two on each side. […] The pieces are then arranged on the corners or angle-points, not on the squares, as in chess or draughts. There are five of these long lines on the board, each containing, of course, nine angle-points […] One point remains unoccupied, the central angle-point of the board […] it is called the foibény ('navel'). […] Second. If there be now no other vacant station between the attacking piece just moved and the enemy's piece along that line, these, whatever their number, are captured at once […] Thirdly. The pieces of the enemy may be captured by a retreat as well as by an advance. […] (b) that he does not take a foe behind him immediately after taking one in front of him, nor one on his right hand immediately after taking on his left hand, and vice versa. 'Don't eat at both ends, like a leech,' says the Malagasy proverb.

records.edition: 1895 first edition
records.supportingPassage: The Korean game of Pa-tok is practically identical with the Chinese game of Wai k'i (Wei ch'i), which is played in Japan under the name of Go. It is played by two players upon a board special to the game, and with two sets of men of different colors. 'The board is divided into squares like a chess-board […] their total number being 324, 18x18. This, however, does not represent the scale of the game, because, as in Chinese chess, the pieces are played on the intersection of the horizontal and vertical lines and not on their intervals. Thus, as there are nineteen lines in either direction, the total number of places on which the men can be played is 19x19, or 361.'

records.supportingPassage: Jackstones are played by boys. Five or seven stones or pieces of brick are used. The game is played upon the ground. There are a great variety of methods. In one, five stones are used. Four are placed upon the ground and one is tossed into the air. Before it falls another is picked up and the one first thrown, which must be caught as it descends, is then put down. The second stone is then tossed and the third picked up, and so on. This is called al-nat-ki, 'laying the eggs.' […] The fifth stone is then tossed up with the right hand, and before it falls one of the other stones is struck under the left hand. This, called al-hpoum-ki, 'setting the eggs,' is repeated until all the stones are struck under the left hand, or the player misses.

[…] when a player is left without seeds in his row of holes on his turn's coming to play, the round is ended. records.supportingPassage: The game requires two players who alternately lay down a small counter — usually a stone or fragment of earthenware — at one of the angles, or the points where the arms of the cross meet the sides of the squares. records.supportingPassage: zohn ahl (zohn, creek; ahl, wood), commonly known as the ahl game: The ahl cloth is divided into points by which the game is counted. […] The space between the parallel lines 1 and 1 and 20 and 20 is called the creek, and the corresponding spaces between the parallel lines at right angles are called the dry branches. records.supportingPassage: Many of the fellaheen of Egypt also frequently amuse themselves with a game called that of the 'seega' […] it consists of a number of holes, generally made in the ground; most commonly, of five rows of five holes in each, or seven rows of seven in each, or nine rows of nine in each […] The holes are called ''oyoon' (or eyes, in the singular ''eyn'). In this seega, they are twenty-five in number. The players have each twelve 'kelbs' […] they then alternately place two kelbs in any of the 'eyns that they may choose, excepting the central 'eyn of the seega. […] The party who begins moves one of his kelbs from a contiguous 'eyn into the central. The other part[y], if the 'eyn now made vacant be not next to any one of those occupied by his kelbs, desires his adversary to give him, or open to him, a way; and the latter must do so, by removing, and thus losing, one of his own kelbs. […] The aim of each party, after the first disposal of the kelbs, is to place any one of his kelbs in such a situation that there shall be, between it and another of his, one of his adversary's kelbs. This, by so doing, he takes; and as long as he can immediately make another capture by such means, he does so, without allowing his adversary to move. — These are the only rules of the game.

records.supportingPassage: Another game very general among the lower classes in Egypt is called 'tab.' […] Four small pieces of stick, of a flat form, about a span (or eight inches) in length […] one side of which, being cut flat and smooth, is white; the other, green […] These are called the 'tab.' Next, it is necessary to be provided with a 'seega.' This is a board, divided into four rows of squares, called 'beyts' […] the beyts are usually seven, nine, eleven, thirteen, or fifteen, in each row. […] If they fall so that one only has its white side upwards, the player is said to have thrown, or brought, 'tab' […] and counts one: if there be two white, and the other two black, he counts two […] if there be three white, and one black, he counts three […] if all four be white, four […] if all four black, six […] When one throws tab, or four, or six, he throws again; but when he has thrown two, or three, it is then the turn of the other. […] Neither party can remove a kelb from its original place but by throwing tab before each such removal. […] Whenever a throw […] enables him to move his kelb into a beyt occupied by one of his opponent's kelbs, he takes the latter. […] thus he may unite any number of his own kelbs, and circulate them together, as if they were but one; but he cannot divide them again […] unless he throw tab. […] Two or more kelbs thus united are called an ''eggeh.'

[…] Two persons, having each of them nine pieces or men, lay them down alternately, one by one, upon the spots […] If a row be formed, he that made it is at liberty to take up one of his competitor's pieces from any part he thinks most to his own advantage, excepting he has made a row, which must not be touched, if he have another piece upon the board that is not a component part of that row. records.supportingPassage: A game known by this name is played with marbles or pegs on a board on which are thirty-three holes […] To play this game there are seventeen pieces called Geese, and another one either larger or distinguished from the Geese by its colour, which is called the Fox. The Fox occupies the centre hole, and the Geese occupy nine holes in front, and four on each side of him. The vacant holes behind are for the Geese and Fox to move in. The game is for the Geese to shut up the Fox so that he cannot move. All the pieces can be moved from one spot to another in the direction of the lines, but cannot pass over two holes at once. The Geese are not permitted to take the Fox. The Fox's business is to take all, or as many of the Geese as will prevent him from being blockaded. The Fox can take the Geese whenever there is a vacant space behind them, which he passes to, then occupies.

Four of the stones were then thrown on the ground; the fifth was thrown up, one stone being picked up from the ground, and the descending fifth stone caught in the same hand […] When he dropped one, he picked it up between his outstretched fingers while the other stones remained on the back of the hand […] This completed one game. records.supportingPassage: This game is usually played by women only, occupying with it their leisure hours. They bet on it such things as beads, dress materials, and other objects of small value […] In preparing the field a spot of ground is leveled and a small flat stone placed in the center. Other stones are then piled around this stone to form a circle […] with four openings, 10 stones being placed in each quarter of the circle, the openings corresponding with the northeast, southeast, southwest, and northwest. […] The counts are as follows: One marked face up counts 2; two marked faces up, 3; three marked faces up, 5; three marked faces down, 10. If the player scores 10, she throws again; otherwise she passes the sticks to the next player. […] The number of players may be two, three, or four […] When more than two play, the two that face each other play as partners. […] If a player's count terminates at, or moves past, a place occupied by an antagonist, she takes her opponent's counting-stick and throws it back, and the latter must start again, losing all her counts. records.supportingPassage: The same name, Ken, is applied in Japan to a large number of games played by two persons with the hands and fingers. One of the commonest of these games is Ishi Ken, or 'Stone ken', usually called Janken. In Ishi Ken the fist is called ishi, 'stone;' the open hand, kami, 'paper,' and the extended index finger and thumb, hasami, 'scissors.' The players extend their hands simultaneously. Stone beats scissors, as scissors will not cut stone. Paper beats stone, as paper will wrap up stone, and scissors beat paper, as scissors cut paper. Janken is often used to decide who shall perform some duty or task. Thus, jinrikisha men play it to determine which is entitled to a passenger. In this case it is customary to cry 'one, two, three,' which is uttered as a thrice-repeated hissing sound before each decisive movement of the hand. […] Mushi Ken, or 'Reptile Ken', is played like Janken. The thumb is called kebi, 'snake;' the forefinger, kairu, 'frog,' and the little finger, namekuji, 'slug.' The snake beats the frog, the frog the slug, and the slug the snake. […] In Kitsune Ken, the two hands slightly bent forward and raised to the ears is called kitsune, 'fox;' the two hands placed on the thighs in the respectful posture, shoya, 'the headman of a village,' and the extended forefinger, teppo, 'gun.' […] kitsune beats shoya, because the fox can deceive the man; the shoya beats teppo, because the gun may not shoot the magistrate, but the teppo beats the kitsune, because the gun kills the fox.
records.supportedClaim: Üç el biçimi ve DÖNGÜSEL üstünlük ilişkisi kaynakta AÇIKÇA verilir: taş makası, kâğıt taşı, makas kâğıdı yener; her üstünlüğün gerekçesi de kaydedilmiştir. Atış eşzamanlıdır ve üç sayımla yapılır. Oyun bir işi kime düşeceğine karar vermek için kullanılır (Culin'in örneği: jinrikişa çekicileri müşteriyi paylaşır). İki bağımsız varyant — Mushi Ken (yılan-kurbağa-sümüklüböcek) ve Kitsune Ken (tilki-muhtar-tüfek) — aynı sayfalarda kural düzeyinde verilir. records.supportingPassage: The jeu forcé (English draughts) only lasted a few years in France and was replaced about 1650 by a variety known as 'Le Grand Forçat'. This also became obsolete within fifty years and was replaced by the game now known as Polish or Continental draughts, first played in the cafés of Paris in 1727. […] Rules 1. The opening position of the pieces is shown in fig. 61. 2. A man moves one square diagonally forwards. 3. A man captures by the short leap both diagonally forwards or backwards. Capturing is compulsory. 4. A king can move diagonally any number of unoccupied squares. 5. A king may land any number of vacant squares beyond a captured piece. Rules 4 and 5 may occur together (a long leap). 6. If a player has a choice of captures he must choose the one in which the greatest number of captures are made, or if equal numbers are at risk, then the more powerful pieces must be taken. 7. records.supportingPassage: FIVE (OR SIX) MEN'S MORRIS. Played on board E. Two players, each with five (or six) men in hand. The men are entered, one at a time, in alternate turns of play, each player endeavouring to form a row along one of the marked lines of the board. Every time a player succeeds in making a row, he takes one of his opponent's men, choosing any man that he likes, and removes it from the board.
